Overview 
 
 
August was the cruellest month for those trading in the precious metals. All of the major 
metals suffered from the same sort of volatility normally only experienced by rhodium. 
Gold took the headlines with a move of almost twenty per cent from its lows to its highs 
followed by a collapse of almost $200 in only two days. Silver and platinum received less 
media attention but moved nearly as far. The palladium price was comparatively stable 
but even this saw changes of more than ten per cent during the month. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Macroeconomic factors buffeted the precious metals sector. Unsurprisingly, therefore, 
gold was the centre of attention with market fundamentals rather less important than  
attitudes towards risk and the desire to hold or divest gold positions. Silver and platinum 
showed a close link to the gold price, as can be seen in the figure above but failed to gain 
from the full safe haven credentials of the yellow metal and consequently underperformed 
it in comparative terms. Palladium was lonely and unloved by investors and showed little 
energy of its own with even the platinum:palladium ratio and positive long term  
fundamentals insufficient to attract buying interest. 
 
At the start of August, the US legislature’s overdue agreement to extend the US debt  
ceiling was announced. With this source of tension removed from the market, gold could 
have retreated but, instead, the news that one of the agencies had downgraded the USA’s 
credit rating spurred a rush to gold in its capacity as a “safe haven” against risk. Gold 
climbed $150 in a week, further aided by a Swiss National Bank decision to inject liquidity 
into its currency in an attempt to make it less attractive to speculators. Weak economic 
data depressed the other precious metals, all of which are more sensitive to industrial  
demand than gold. 
 
On the 8th of August, gold moved above platinum, forcing some investors into action to 
trade this price ratio. Historically, platinum has rarely traded below gold and, whatever the 
rationale, trading this ratio has generally been profitable. It was not surprising therefore 
when platinum started to follow gold higher as it continued upwards, aided by a challeng-
ing industrial relations climate within the South African mining industry. For the rest of the 
month, platinum largely ignored the impact of further negative economic developments 
and accompanied gold instead. Silver essentially plotted the same course as platinum and 
gold from here on in, with its precious character outweighing the industrial aspect of its 
behaviour. Palladium slowly gained ground but showed little link to the other metals. 
 
Fresh concerns over European sovereign debt – French this time – drove gold over 
$1,800 for the first time ever on the 11th of August. With the gold price apparently spiralling 
out of control, margins were increased on the Shanghai Gold Exchange and on COMEX 
that day, driving gold back $50 below its peak with silver and platinum weakening too.

Interestingly, the US Federal Reserve’s comments that interest rates would remain low 
into 2013 drove a greater acceptance of risk and a small sell-off of gold, suggesting that 
QE3, should it happen, might be less positive for gold than for some other assets. 
 
Later, weak European economic data restarted gold’s move higher. Gold powered to a 
new record $1,910 and above as stock markets tumbled due to these woes. Platinum and 
silver followed. However, the market was over-extended at this point and further margin 
increases on the same two exchanges on the 25th drove strong selling, forcing gold 
roughly $200 lower in only two days. Platinum and silver followed. Comments by some 
people that this marked the end for the “gold bubble” seem to have been rather  
premature, however, with gold recovering much of the recently-lost ground in moving to 
end the month at $1,825, taking its new friends along for the journey. 
 
 
Quantitative easing – QE3 
 
The QE3 debate has started much as the QE2 debate started in Q3 2010 following the US 
Federal Reserve’s annual Jackson Hole meeting. The background for this speculation is, 
as it was last year, a proliferation of weak economic data. Worryingly, though, on this  
occasion, it is not just the USA that is suffering. Consumer confidence is weak throughout 
much of Europe and North America with inflation outpacing both interest rates and pay 
awards and eroding consumers’ purchasing power. Economic growth in China and some 
of the other developing nations is also weakening. Given that this has been one of the 
most important factors in supporting the global economy, this has led the market to worry 
about the short to medium term future. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
However, America remains the focus for most investors. With the Federal Reserve ex-
pressing its view that unemployment remains stubbornly high, the market has come to the 
realisation that something has to be done. A consensus seems to be developing that this 
will be quantitative easing, so-called QE3. Arguments abound as to whether QE and QE2 
were successful or not. However, with other approaches such as the provision of tax re-
bates or the writing off of a portion of home loans taking longer to affect the economy, 
QE3 may appear to be a more attractive option. 
 
The environment is, though, perhaps not as welcoming for QE3 as it was for QE2: the po-
litical debate within the USA has turned against quantitative easing, making it more chal-
lenging to restart this process. It is also not clear that reducing bond yields and interest 
rates is the key to stimulating lending and kick-starting the economy: with unemployment 
stubbornly high, economic output weak and many home-owners still “under water”, there 
seems little reason to borrow money to use for normal economic purposes. Additionally, 
there are signs of nascent inflation in many countries, suggesting that greater care must 
be taken in timing the withdrawal of any stimulus.

Nonetheless, while there are many other actions that could be taken in order to stimulate 
the economy, we expect that some degree of quantitative easing will occur in the USA. It 
is likely to be smaller than the previous rounds, it may be targeted differently and it may 
go by a different name but we expect to see QE3 arrive at some point later this year or 
early next year. There may be more effective actions that could be taken (for instance re-
purchasing distressed stock in the housing market and demolishing it) but the immediacy 
of quantitative easing and the fact that it is within the control of the Federal Reserve are 
likely to make QE an attractive option. There is also increasing chatter over the prospects 
for launching further QE in the UK. We would not be surprised to see this happen and feel 
it should add to the upwards pressure on precious metals prices. 
 
In terms of price expectations, we see QE3 as having a similar, but perhaps smaller, im-
pact to that of QE2. The prices of silver and palladium both started to move higher as 
speculation that QE2 would take place increased in Q3 2010 (platinum and gold benefited 
too but to a lesser extent). When the programme was finally launched, the impact on 
prices was, if anything, less substantial than from the initial expectation of more QE. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
However, we note that other asset prices (including the base metals) have struggled in 
recent weeks and we interpret this as meaning that the market has not yet started to price 
in concrete expectations of QE3. As further QE becomes more likely, a range of asset 
prices should start to rise, including the precious metals. As a result, we feel that further 
economic weakness which makes QE more palatable in the short term should be benefi-
cial for the prices of all of the precious metals to some degree.

The death of safe havens 
 
Just as the demise of Bear Stearns made many investors more aware of the distinctions 
between banks in terms of their creditworthiness, the continued struggles of the global 
economy have reminded people of the value of safe havens. Gold has benefited as the 
“safest” of “safe havens”. While its value may ebb and flow, in the extreme case of the end 
of civilised society, enough people believe that a gold coin will retain some value.  
However, assuming that society does not break down, there is a wider range of possible 
“safe havens” in which to invest. 
 
Historically, there are relatively few assets which are viewed as safe in times of market 
stress. These would normally include gold, and to a lesser extent silver, a few currencies 
including the Swiss Franc and the Dollar and a range of bonds of the major nations,  
principally including Germany, Japan and the USA. Many of these have performed  
relatively well during the most recent phase of the economic crisis in their role of capital 
preservation (with the US Dollar the main exception). 
 
However, as the correlations between different asset classes have increased, the ideal 
“safe haven” investment has become more difficult to find. Historically, the shares of the 
gold miners have been used as a proxy for the gold price and therefore a safe haven. 
However, over recent months as the global economy has started to wilt, gold has  
outperformed these shares. There are a number of possible causes for this divergence 
(including cost control, gearing and forecasts of future price declines) but we believe that 
this primarily reflects an unselective view of all equities as risky assets and the physical 
metal as a place of safety.

The recent downgrading of the US credit rating (at the start of August) means that what 
would typically be viewed as a risk-free asset cannot now be viewed in quite the same 
way. The travails of many of the Eurozone governments over debt issues have placed 
question marks over the health of the Euro too. German bonds remain attractive  
compared to other European bonds but the uncertain future for the Euro makes these an 
interesting choice as a safe haven. Nonetheless, in recent weeks as concern over global 
growth has intensified, even these imperfect “safeish havens” have attracted capital  
inflows with yields falling substantially. 
 
The Swiss Franc saw similar “benefits” as a safe haven throughout the first half of 2011. 
In fact, it looked like a slightly more attractive version of gold, with an interest rate and a 
lower haircut when used as collateral. In Swiss Franc terms, gold barely moved  
throughout that period. 
 
However, at the start of August, the Swiss National Bank announced its first plan to flood 
the market with liquidity. This started to make it clear to investors that the Franc is just like 
any other currency in that it can be created at will. Unsurprisingly, it was sold off with 
XAUCHF rising from 1,300 to 1,500 demonstrating a clear preference for gold over this 
new “slightly safe haven” of the CHF. Looking at the 6th September Swiss announcement 
that it intended to buy “unlimited quantities” of foreign currency in order to peg their  
currency to the Euro, the jump of over 100 in XAUCHF merely reinforces the fact that safe 
havens are fewer in number than they were before. With plenty of economic turbulence to 
come in the next few months, the need for capital preservation seems unlikely to diminish 
quickly and the gold price seems set to appreciate as the best of a bad set of choices for 
this role.

Gold 
How best to describe the movements of the gold price during August? A rapid climb from 
$1,610 to a closing $1,825, an increase of 13.4 per cent? A continuation of a ten year-long 
bull run? The first stages of a bubble? A series of new all-time nominal highs recorded up 
to $1,912 or a $200 fall from the highs in just two days which taught investors a valuable 
lesson? All of these and more would give an accurate description of at least one facet of 
gold’s price performance throughout the month. 
 
To give some perspective, gold had traded around the $1,500-$1,550 level for most of the 
months of May and June, ending June weakly with the cessation of the second round of 
US quantitative easing (QE2) making investors more wary than they had previously been. 
Since that point, the gold price has been rising for much of the time, reaching $1,615, it-
self a nominal record price, at the end of July and a peak of $1,912 on the 23rd of August. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The driving forces for this upwards movement in the price appear to have been simple 
and numerous. As has been the case throughout this year, consumers, whether Euro-
pean, Chinese or Indian have continued to buy gold as an investment and a hedge 
against risk. The macroeconomic environment continued to disappoint too: slowing growth 
in North America was accompanied by a worsening outlook for the Chinese economy. 
July saw the price driven still higher by concerns that a dysfunctional US government 
might not extend its debt ceiling in time to avoid defaulting on some of its obligations.  
 
However, as soon as this issue was solved, other worries took its place: a sign of a bullish 
market. The downgrade of the US credit rating damaged the attractiveness of the US Dol-
lar as a home for nervous capital. The first stage of intervention by the Swiss National 
Bank at the start of August weakened the Franc and removed another safe haven, adding 
to the attraction of gold. A general lack of belief in the ability or desire of European leaders 
to address Eurozone debt issues increased risk aversion and drove gold onward. And, to 
cap this all, the first signs of renewed debate on the advisability of launching QE3 in 
America (and other QE elsewhere in the world) started to emerge in late August. 
 
Throughout almost all of this period the gold price rose. However, the ride upwards was 
not smooth: gold tumbled from $1,815 on the 11th to $1,725 on the 12th as both the 
Shanghai Gold Exchange and COMEX increased margin requirements on their contracts. 
The respite was only temporary and, with the price moving over $1,900 on the 22nd, the 
imposition of yet higher margins on both exchanges drove some panicked selling which 
ended with the price crashing to $1,705 just two days later. The price recovered to $1,820 
by the end of the month, keeping the bullish trend intact and leaving one to wonder just 
where gold would have been at that point without the margin changes.

Futures margins 
 
Margins on the various gold contracts on the Shanghai Gold Exchange were raised twice 
during August as speculative interest overheated in the run up to new all-time record 
prices. Margins were raised to 11 per cent on all the gold contracts at the close on the 11th 
of August and to 12 per cent at the end of trading on the 25th of August in an attempt to 
cool market interest.  
 
Likewise, margins were raised on gold contracts on COMEX on the 11th and 25th. The two 
major falls in the gold price during the month of August appear to have been triggered by 
these margin increases which reduced the maximum leverage available on a futures  
position, in effect making it more expensive to hold. This should act as a reminder to  
investors that the futures exchanges and regulators will not necessarily stand by and  
simply watch prices accelerate upwards. However, given that these downwards  
movements were artificially triggered (i.e. not initially caused by changes in investor or 
consumer attitude or behaviour) this suggests that bullish sentiment persists. 
 
 
Official sector activity 
 
Central Bank buying of gold continues. The most recent data released concerns July and 
reveals that both Russia and Colombia were net buyers of metal during that month. Rus-
sia’s buying was not at all surprising as it purchased another 4.4 tonnes from domestic 
production, taking its reserves to 841 tonnes. Reports suggest that we may see further 
buying in the weeks ahead. Colombia’s decision was more surprising in that it was the first 
purchase by that country for more than ten years. The amount of metal bought (2.3 ton-
nes, taking reserves to a total of 9.1 tonnes) was relatively insignificant but the change in 
mindset from yet another central bank suggests that reserve diversification through gold is 
now a mainstream activity in the official sector. 
 
Additionally, a widely circulated report seems to suggest that China is buying gold for its 
reserves. Unfortunately, the information in the report itself dates from the first half of 2009, 
suggesting that it may not be all that current. Nonetheless, we fully understand and agree 
with the rationale for why China should be purchasing gold. The lack of updated data on 
Chinese official sector gold holdings makes any comments on this subject speculative by 
their very nature. However, although we discount this report, we would be surprised if 
China is not buying gold and we believe that this is bullish for the gold price both in the 
short term and whenever such buying is eventually revealed publicly. 
 
Interestingly, though, two countries apparently reduced their holdings of gold during the 
month of July. This selling has been relatively rare in recent months but, nonetheless,  
Kazakhstan sold 3.1 tonnes of gold while Tajikistan disposed of 1.2 tonnes of gold. More 
importantly, despite speculation over the matter, no significant selling of gold was reported 
by any European bank despite the ongoing debt crisis there. 
 
Elsewhere, the Venezuelan Government announced its plans to nationalise the local gold 
industry. Venezuela is a relatively small producer of gold from either the formal or informal 
mining sector but this type of government intervention is at least marginally bullish for gold 
as nationalisation tends to have a negative impact on mine output. The Government has 
also decided to repatriate its gold reserves from overseas vaults in case any attempts are 
made to seize its assets. Its total metal holdings are 365.8 tonnes, which is not  
insignificant. However, we do not expect this individual action to have any significant  
impact on the gold market. 
 
 
US coin sales and ETF investment 
 
Sales of gold coins by the US Mint climbed from between 60,000 and 65,000 ounces in 
each of June and July to 112,000 ounces in August. This is the highest August figure

since 1999 and could reflect heightened fears over the economic situation. However, 
monthly sales are somewhat “lumpy” and we feel it is more informative to focus on rolling 
six month or cumulative year-to-date sales. These sales are running close to but below 
the level of 2010 and 2009 although they are substantially higher than in previous years, 
illustrating investors' focus on risk aversion following the global economic crisis (or the first 
phase of the global economic crisis for the pessimists amongst us). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Interestingly, the six month running rate of sales is below 90,000 ounces per month, lower 
than at almost any point since early 2008. We feel that this weakening interest reflects 
some price sensitivity by numismatists but it also reflects the reality that the most risk-
averse or risk-aware investors have already put a proportion of their assets into physical 
gold. Consequently, there are fewer investors remaining who wish to buy physical metal in 
this form and demand is weakening. However, we do not feel that this is illustrative of a 
fall in investor interest in gold as an asset: other forms of gold investment may be viewed 
more as part of a portfolio and flows of money into these – as opposed to gold as a hedge 
against disaster – should continue in the current environment. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
By way of illustration, we believe that ETF investment is a better indicator of professional 
or fund investor interest. ETF flows were very strong in July with more than one million 
ounces purchased in three of the four weeks that month. However, they slowed during 
August before suffering a remarkable outflow of over 2 million ounces as the price slid 
roughly $200 late in the month. This should act as a reminder that the hands of many of 
these investors are not as “sticky” as conventional wisdom believes. Just as interestingly, 
the buying activity that is seen (or more properly, the net buying activity that is seen) is 
markedly different to physical interest in coins.

In contrast to coin purchasing, ETF flows are much more intermittent, appearing at times 
of significant market stress in recent years. The previous peaks in metal purchasing via 
this route were at the time of the Bear Stearns bankruptcy and the first signs of European 
sovereign debt issues. The recent upsurge in buying interest suggests that these larger 
investors are becoming greatly concerned over the unhealthy state of the world economy. 
It is noteworthy that net flows into gold contracts on COMEX have shown a similar pattern, 
with the exception of the duration of QE2, confirming our view that institutional investors 
are responsible for most of the changes in ETF holdings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Real and nominal record prices and targets 
 
During August, gold recorded a series of all-time nominal record prices as it has repeat-
edly done throughout the past year. With the price in uncharted territory, there are rela-
tively few upside targets still available for investors. Of course, the big round figure num-
bers remain as possible attractors of interest: $2,000 per ounce, a figure that might have 
seemed outlandish only a few years ago seems to be the first major target and numerous 
market commentators have started to point out longer term targets of anywhere from 
$2,500 to $5,000. Setting aside any arguments of whether this overt and extreme bullish-
ness is justified and whether gold is in a bubble, we think it is interesting to view the cur-
rent prices in real rather than nominal terms.

South African mining sector. In the platinum industry, these typically take place every two 
years and discussions can be fractious, providing some support for the price of this metal.

reached agreement with the National Union of Miners in early September without any 
strike action occurring. There was a short-lived strike at ARM and Norilsk Nickel’s Nkomati 
joint venture but there have been few other strikes as yet across the industry. 
 
Although discussions continue at a number of producers and more strikes may yet occur, 
the likelihood of widespread disruption appears to be receding and this source of support 
for the platinum price should weaken. Of longer term relevance, the wage deals agreed so 
far have tended to be for annual increases approaching ten per cent. This is inflationary 
and can only lead to higher platinum production costs and prices in the future.

Zimbabwe, including the three active platinum mines. All of the companies concerned

num’s Unki mine. However, the minister responsible did comment on the other two mines, 
stating that he believed that agreement could be reached on Mimosa.

expect this matter to be clarified quickly. We do expect an agreement to be reached,

Palladium investment 
 
Investors largely ignored palladium in August after the sharp fall in its price at the start of 
the month. As had been the case following its previous declines, palladium bounced well 
but, on this occasion, it ran out of momentum before reaching $800. This apathy and ero-
sion of interest can be seen both in Exchange Traded Fund (ETF) flows and futures activ-
ity on NYMEX. 
 
ETF holdings of palladium reached a peak of 2.43 million ounces in February 2011 but 
now stand at only 2.13 million ounces. The outflows of metal continued in August with al-
most 100,000 ounces sold (most of it by American investors) in the week following the 
early August price fall. The selling has now developed into a clear and persistent trend 
with net redemptions seen in nine of the last twelve weeks.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
On NYMEX, open interest decreased by a fifth during August to 2.04 million contracts. Net 
long speculative positions fell from 1.89 million ounces to 1.36 million ounces as long po-
sitions were liquidated. While this has led to an uninspiring price performance, this is not 
an overextended position for palladium and it seems better protected from investor-driven 
sell-offs than the other precious metals.

Automotive demand 
 
With world economic output slowing and even previously quickly-growing economies such 
as Brazil and China beginning to struggle, car sales and output are set to disappoint this 
year, with palladium and rhodium demand being lower than had initially been expected. 
Demand will, nonetheless, be higher than in 2010 as the market is still growing. 
 
In Japan, vehicle output has recovered well from the earthquake, tsunami and nuclear 
accident. It has not yet returned to normal but should do so in September. H1 2011 output 
was 3.43 million units, 1.4 million lower than a year earlier due to the impact of the disas-
ter. According to Toyota, it now plans to produce and sell 2.79 million cars in Japan during 
the calendar year (in addition to units produced by its Hino and Daihatsu subsidiaries). 
This is 310,000 units lower than was forecast at the start of the year. However, it is some 
140,000 units higher than was forecast during June, demonstrating that the supply chain 
has recovered more quickly than was initially expected. It is worth noting that the original 
production target for the year was already lower than the 2010 figure, reflecting concern 
over weak domestic demand and the impact of a strong Yen. At Nissan, first half Japa-
nese production decreased by 18 per cent year-on-year but output in June was, remarka-
bly, higher than a year earlier and almost back to normal levels. Honda’s recovery to nor-
mal production levels within Japan should be complete in Q3 too. 
 
The North American market is still rather sickly. August sales were broadly acceptable but 
the annualised running rate is now 12.1 million units, substantially weaker than the 13 mil-
lion figure at the start of the year. With many indicators (such as the Purchasing Manager 
Indices) pointing to a slower US economy in the second half of the year, there must be 
some prospect of sales falling below this figure. On a more positive note, oil prices have 
fallen and may mitigate some of the consumer preference that has developed for smaller, 
cheaper to operate cars which use less palladium and rhodium in their catalysts. Addition-
ally, incentives available to purchasers of new cars fell by 6.1 per cent in August to $2,615 
per vehicle as the US automakers made the most of a lack of competition from their Japa-
nese competitors. It seems likely that, as Japanese models become more widely avail-
able, competition will increase in this marketplace and incentives will increase once again. 
This should attract additional consumers and we are therefore a little more positive than 
the consensus forecast for the outlook for the remainder of this year. 
 
Sales are, though, still expected to remain relatively weak as the US struggles to avoid a 
double dip recession. Falling consumer confidence, higher fuel prices and lower  
incentives have all taken their toll. Fleet sales weakened throughout the second quarter 
and are now running level with year earlier figures, having been significantly ahead of Q1 
2010 in the first quarter of this year. We take this as a negative for automotive palladium 
demand and a worrying signal of worsening business confidence. However, high second 
hand vehicle prices have driven some consumers to purchase new rather than used  
vehicles, providing some additional sales. 
 
Finally, in China, The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers now expects vehi-
cle sales to rise by roughly 5 per cent this year. Our expectation is that the market will out-
perform this target as the Chinese Government intervenes to keep the economy growing 
quickly. July passenger vehicle sales were 1.01 million units, lower than the June figure 
due to normal seasonal factors but almost 7 per cent more than in July 2010. There are 
already signs that Chinese automotive demand could accelerate in H2. China continues to 
add vehicles to the list of those eligible for its environmental subsidies. It also revealed a 
plan to pay consumers up to 18,000 RMB (roughly US$2,750) if they scrap a car that is 
between 6 and 15 years old and purchase a new car in 2011. 
 
Despite differential taxation in favour of smaller cars, sales of larger sports utility vehicles 
continue to outpace growth in the rest of this market, with 20 per cent more sold in July 
2011 than in July 2010. Forecasts are for SUV sales to approach US levels by the end of 
the decade. Overall, vehicle sizes and engine sizes are increasing, leading to higher metal 
loadings within China.
